title: Art Forms in Nature, Plate 74: Orchidae

image.credit: collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: Several orchid flowers and buds are arranged on a single page, with ruffled petals, curling lips and stems that bend in different directions. The blossoms vary in shape and size and are set together in a decorative pattern.

source.museum: collection not stated on source page

context: A lithography print made by Ernst Haeckel in 1904 as one plate in his Art Forms in Nature series. Orchidae is the Latin name for the orchid family, plants known for flowers with unusual, often symmetrical shapes.

descriptions.k: These are orchid flowers. Their petals are curly and frilly. Look at the different flower shapes. Which flower would you smell first? What do you think it smells like?
descriptions.g12: Ernst Haeckel drew these orchids, which are flowers with fancy petals. Some petals curl, some ruffle and some stick out like lips. The flowers are different shapes and sizes. Which orchid looks the strangest to you? What makes it look that way?
descriptions.g35: Ernst Haeckel made this lithography print of orchids, called Orchidae, in 1904. It is Plate 74 from his Art Forms in Nature series. He placed many blossoms and buds on one page so you can compare them. Choose two orchids. How are their petals alike, and how are they different?
descriptions.g68: Plate 74 (1904) shows the orchid family, Orchidae, as a comparison of flower forms. Haeckel arranges blossoms and buds so that you can study shape, symmetry and variety, while the page also reads as a balanced design. Lithography records delicate detail in petals and stems. How does the layout help you compare the flowers, and what does it do for the look of the page?
descriptions.g910: In Plate 74 of Art Forms in Nature (1904), Haeckel presents Orchidae as a catalogue of variation. Symmetrical flowers, curling petals and stems are placed to create rhythm across the sheet, so the plate works as scientific record and as ornament. How does the arrangement direct your attention from bloom to bloom, and where do decorative choices seem to outweigh documentary ones? Consider how repetition and variation guide your answer.
descriptions.g1112: Plate 74 (1904) shows Orchidae in a format that blends botanical study with design. Haeckel's arrangement stresses symmetry, variation and the intricate forms of the flowers, and lithography gives them fine, delicate surfaces. The series has been read alongside the visual culture of its time, and Haeckel's broader ideas remain debated. How does the plate's beauty shape the authority of its scientific message? Weigh what the careful arrangement adds to, or takes from, its credibility.

teacherNote.context: A lithography print from 1904 by Ernst Haeckel showing orchids, grouped under the Latin name Orchidae. The plate is part of the Art Forms in Nature series.
directions: Have students draw one orchid by folding a paper in half and drawing the matching sides, then discuss where symmetry helps and where nature varies.
Ask students to compare two blooms on the plate and write three differences in petal shape.
Discuss why a scientist might choose a drawing over a photograph and what each can show.
